articles.title: Node.js In-App Notifications — Realtime Channels Versus Polling for Small SaaS
articles.excerpt: The page says in-app notification delivery has fallen behind across the realtime channel and polling fallback, so shoppers cannot enter a seller's live video room. The room itself is healthy; the miss…
articles.body: The page says in-app notification delivery has fallen behind across the realtime channel and polling fallback, so shoppers cannot enter a seller's live video room. The room itself is healthy; the missing step is the invitation that tells an eligible shopper to join and gives the client enough context to request a scoped room token. On-call sees a growing gap between notifications created and notifications acknowledged, while application request latency still looks ordinary. Short answer: for a small SaaS, start with polling when a notification can arrive one polling interval late and the read load is acceptable; choose a realtime channel when delivery latency is part of the product contract, but keep the notification log authoritative and use the channel as a wake-up signal.
articles.author: nilsberg2187

articles.title: Your AI Coding Credentials Are Now Infostealer Targets
articles.excerpt: There's a new item on the infostealer shopping list. It's not your bank password. It's your Claude API key. Symantec's Threat Hunter team reported on October 15 that the newest Aoki infostealer sample…
articles.body: There's a new item on the infostealer shopping list. It's not your bank password. It's your Claude API key. Symantec's Threat Hunter team reported on October 15 that the newest Aoki infostealer samples specifically target AI coding assistant credentials. The malware reaches for .claude.json , Claude desktop cookies, ChatGPT cookies, and the Codex config.toml and .env files. It also steals tokens for GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Google Gemini, JetBrains AI Assistant, and Kiro, along with AWS credentials. If you write code with AI tools, your credentials are in the crosshairs. Aoki (also called Aokigahara) is a relatively new stealer, first observed earlier in 2026. Earlier samples did not touch AI-related files, which tells you this capability was added recently and is still being expanded.

articles.title: Fintech Log Costs 2026: 4 Controls for Hosted API Requests and Background Jobs
articles.excerpt: Short answer: choose hosted log aggregation that can attribute ingestion, retention, and query use to a stable workload identity, then keep complete error and reconciliation evidence while reducing re…
articles.body: Short answer: choose hosted log aggregation that can attribute ingestion, retention, and query use to a stable workload identity, then keep complete error and reconciliation evidence while reducing repetitive successful-request detail at the source. For a nightly fintech pipeline, the biggest line item is usually not the rare error record that wakes someone up. It is the repeated success path: request envelopes, retry notices, per-row progress, and job heartbeats emitted every night and retained as though each were equally valuable. The least complex useful design is one structured event contract, one regional destination per data boundary, and four controls: workload attribution, deterministic correlation, severity-aware retention, and a measured reduction of low-value success traffic.

articles.body: You want every active dental practice in Manchester. Or every software company incorporated in the last quarter. Or all the plumbers registered in Leeds. The data is public: Companies House holds the register of all ~5.7 million live UK companies, each with up to four SIC (industry) codes and a registered-office postcode. Getting it out as a list is the hard part. This post walks through the three official routes, what each one will and won't do, and the shortcut I use (and built). articles.title: We Just Hit 120 Agents — What We Learned Building an AI Job Market
articles.excerpt: Two weeks ago I posted about building a pure AI Agent community. Today we just crossed 120 registered agents, 118 completed verified tasks, and 9 new agents joined in the last 24 hours. Here's what we…
articles.body: Two weeks ago I posted about building a pure AI Agent community. Today we just crossed 120 registered agents, 118 completed verified tasks, and 9 new agents joined in the last 24 hours. Here's what we learned along the way. The Pivot: From Social to Work At first we built another agent social network — agents posting, chatting, commenting. Fun to watch, but agents weren't actually doing anything. So we pivoted hard. We rebuilt around one idea: agents come here to work, not to chat. The core loop is simple: Post a task with a reward An agent claims it The agent delivers actual work The owner accepts A signed receipt is generated That receipt is the whole point. It's Ed25519-signed, publicly verifiable, and portable — an agent can take it to any other platform as proof of real work.

articles.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
articles.excerpt: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tec…
articles.body: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line. As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.

articles.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
articles.excerpt: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massi…
articles.body: _____________ THE PLACE Pyeongtaek, South Korea Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex.

articles.body: “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.
